cards.front: How is sprint speed classically defined, and what underlying physiological factor determines an athlete's ability to maximize it?
cards.back:
Classical Equation:
$$\text{Sprint Speed} = \text{Stride Length} \times \text{Stride Frequency}$$.

Underlying Limiting Factor: While sprint speed can logically be increased by expanding stride length or elevating stride frequency, both variables are fundamentally governed by rapid force production into the ground (Rate of Force Development, RFD) and proper biomechanical force application.

cards.tag: Vertical Force Application & Elite vs. Novice Distinction
cards.front: What single kinetic component represents the most critical differentiator between elite and novice sprinters?
cards.back: The magnitude of vertical force applied to the ground during the stance phase is the primary differentiator. Furthermore, elite sprinters distinguish themselves by applying these greater vertical forces in the shortest possible duration (demonstrating an extremely high rate of force development, RFD).

cards.front: What does stride length represent biomechanically, and how does it quantitatively differ between elite and novice male sprinters at maximum velocity?
cards.back:
Biomechanical Meaning: Stride length represents the horizontal displacement of an athlete's body mass during the flight phase resulting from ground reaction forces.

Quantitative Comparison:
  • Elite Male Sprinters: Achieve a stride length of 2.70 m at maximum velocity.
  • Novice Sprinters: Achieve a stride length of 2.56 m at maximum velocity.

cards.tag: Stride Rate, Ground Contact Time, and Flight Kinetics
cards.front: How do stride frequency and ground contact time differ between elite and novice sprinters, and why do faster sprinters spend more time in the air?
cards.back:
• Stride Rate: Elite male sprinters produce stride rates near 4.63 steps/s, compared to 4.43 steps/s in novice sprinters.
  • Ground Contact Time: Faster sprinters require less ground contact time to exert the force needed to displace body mass.
  • Flight Time: Because elite sprinters spend less time on the ground during each stance phase, they spend a greater proportion of total sprinting time in the air.

cards.tag: Swing Leg Kinematics: Recovery Time Constancy
cards.front: Does faster swing leg turnover in the air distinguish elite sprinters from novice sprinters?
cards.back: No. Research demonstrates that the time required to reposition the swing leg through the air in preparation for the subsequent ground contact is virtually identical between elite sprinters and their slower counterparts. Elite sprinting speed is determined by stance phase ground force production, not swing leg speed during flight.

cards.tag: Knee Recovery Height & Front-Loaded Force Production (Mann's Model)
cards.front: According to Mann, how does knee height at maximal flexion of the recovering leg facilitate elite sprint velocity?
cards.back:
An optimized, high knee position provides two decisive mechanical advantages:
  • It creates a greater vertical excursion and time period for force production and subsequent ground clearance.
  • It enables properly directed downward vertical forces, allowing elite sprinters to produce the vast majority of their ground force within the first half of the stance phase, propelling elite male sprinters to velocities near 12.55 m/s (versus 11.25 m/s in novices).

cards.tag: Subtasks and Structural Phases of Linear Sprinting
cards.front: What are the three distinct subtasks of linear sprinting, and how are the stance and flight phases segmented?
cards.back:
Three Sprint Subtasks: The Start, Acceleration, and Top Speed (Maximum Velocity).

Phase Segmentation:
  • Stance Phase (Support): An initial eccentric braking period followed immediately by a concentric propulsive period.
  • Flight Phase: The recovery segment (hip and knee flexion) and the ground preparation segment of the swing leg prior to foot strike.

cards.front: How do posture and mechanical mechanisms differ between the acceleration phase and the maximum-velocity phase of a sprint?
cards.back:
• Acceleration Phase: Forward-inclined posture; large propulsive horizontal forces drive acceleration and progressively elevate the hips above the ground until speed gains taper off.
  • Maximum-Velocity Phase: Upright posture; the athlete utilizes the stretch–shortening cycle (SSC) through active musculotendinous stiffness regulation to maintain horizontal center-of-mass momentum down the track.

cards.tag: Technical Coaching Errors & The Overstriding Fallacy
cards.front: What causes overstriding during sprinting, and why is it mechanically detrimental to running speed?
cards.back:
Causes: Flawed coaching cues (e.g., reaching for successively longer marks on the track to gain speed) or an athlete consciously attempting to "catch up" to a competitor.

Detriments: Landing with the foot placed excessively far in front of the center of mass causes severe braking forces, prolongs ground contact time, disrupts natural gait cycle mechanics, and substantially increases hamstring strain injury risk.

cards.tag: Fundamental Training Objectives for Speed Development
cards.front: What are the primary training objectives for developing sprint speed, and what role do weightlifting movements play?
cards.back:
Primary Training Objectives:
  1. Emphasize Brief Ground Support Times: Cultivates rapid stride rates by developing high-velocity RFD and explosive strength.
  2. Overload the Stretch–Shortening Cycle (SSC): Maximizes the amplitude of impulse generated during each foot contact.
Role of Weightlifting: Complete Olympic weightlifting movements and their derivatives (cleans, snatches, jerks, and pulls) are essential exercises that overload the SSC with forces greater than those produced during an unresisted open sprint.
